abs-equations.why: ~|x| = 5~ asks which numbers sit 5 away from zero, and two do. That is why absolute value equations usually split into two cases: the inside is ~+5~ or the inside is ~-5~.
traps: An absolute value can never equal a negative, so ~|x - 3| = -2~ has no solution — see that before doing algebra.
~|x| = 0~ has exactly one solution. Three cases worth knowing on sight: positive gives two, zero gives one, negative gives none.

abs-inequalities.why: Less-than means close to zero, so the inside is trapped between ~-k~ and ~k~ — one interval, an *and*. Greater-than means far from zero in either direction — two separate pieces, an *or*. Getting that distinction right is the whole topic.
traps: ~|x| > 3~ is not ~-3 < x < 3~. It is ~x < -3~ *or* ~x > 3~, which is the outside, not the inside.
Tolerances in engineering are written exactly this way: ~|measured - target| \le 0.5~.

abs-graphs.why: The graph of ~y = |x|~ is a V, because the negative half gets reflected upward. Everything you know about shifting and stretching applies to it, and the corner sits at the vertex ~(h, k)~ in ~y = a|x - h| + k~.
traps: The sign inside the bars flips: ~|x + 4|~ has its corner at ~x = -4~.
A negative ~a~ turns the V upside down, making the vertex a maximum rather than a minimum.
